claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys is governed by a balance between configurational-entropy stabilization and segregation-driven phase formation.
High configurational entropy favors a single disordered matrix in this alloy system.
An inherent tendency for elemental segregation, especially between Cr and Co, promotes ordered or brittle secondary phases.
An optimal Cr-to-Co ratio minimizes segregation-driven ordering and maintains a robust single-phase microstructure.
Retention of a single-phase microstructure underpins the combined high-temperature strength, oxidation resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni has a predominantly single-phase ordered-B2 or disordered-BCC starting microstructure after standard casting or annealing.
Changing the Cr-to-Co ratio while holding the other elements constant will alter phase stability.
Annealing temperature influences decomposition and its characteristic length scale.
Grain-boundary state and local chemical short-range order determine whether the alloy remains single-phase or develops nanoscale precipitates or ordered regions.
Atomic-size differences and mixing-enthalpy disparities between Cr and Co control whether the alloy remains single-phase or segregates and orders.
Secondary phases produced by Cr/Co-driven segregation are often more brittle than the initial matrix.
Composition-dependent B2+BCC decomposition affects mechanical behavior.
Microstructural evolution associated with decomposition dictates mechanical integrity under extreme temperatures and irradiation.
An optimal Cr-to-Co ratio will yield a stable single phase together with high-temperature strength, corrosion resistance, radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness.
Increasing Cr beyond a critical threshold will promote secondary-phase formation.
Cr-induced secondary-phase formation will degrade mechanical properties, oxidation resistance, and radiation tolerance relative to the equiatomic baseline.
The equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni baseline exhibits a high-entropy single phase.
The proposed mechanism applies only where diffusion and thermal exposure permit segregation to develop.
Compositions far from the baseline or extreme processing conditions may activate additional phase-stability mechanisms.
